title: The Hormuz Effect: How a War in the Gulf Pushed Singapore Past the UAE as India's Second-Largest Export Market
excerpt: A 180 per cent surge in exports to Singapore and a 36 per cent collapse in UAE-bound shipments tell the story of a trade map being redrawn in real time by conflict, insurance premiums and supply-chain panic.
body:
For years, India's export geography followed a predictable pattern: the United States on top, the United Arab Emirates in second place, and a cluster of European and Asian markets jostling behind. In April 2026, that hierarchy cracked.

## A seismic shift in one month

Data released by India's Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence show that Singapore leapfrogged the UAE to become India's second-largest export destination in April. Exports to Singapore surged 180 per cent year-on-year, reaching $3.20 billion. In the same month, exports to the UAE fell 36 per cent to $2.18 billion — the sharpest single-month decline since the Covid lockdown of 2020.

The cause is no mystery. The ongoing conflict near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes, has upended shipping economics in the Persian Gulf. War-risk insurance premiums for vessels transiting the strait have tripled since January. Container lines have rerouted cargo. Some Indian exporters have simply stopped booking Gulf-bound shipments altogether.

## Singapore as the new clearing house

Singapore's rise is not accidental. The city-state has long functioned as a re-export hub, but the Hormuz crisis has accelerated its role as a clearing house for goods that would otherwise move through Jebel Ali or Fujairah. Indian refineries, petrochemical producers and electronics exporters have redirected volumes through Singapore's port and bonded warehouses, where insurance costs are a fraction of Gulf-route rates.

The shift is also structural. India's bilateral trade with ASEAN has deepened since the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership negotiations, and Singapore serves as the financial gateway. Indian IT services firms, many of which maintain Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore, are routing a larger share of project revenue through their Singaporean entities.

## The pain for the diaspora

For the 3.5 million Indians living in the Gulf, the trade disruption is personal. The UAE economy, heavily reliant on logistics and re-export activity, has seen port throughput at Jebel Ali decline for three consecutive months. Several free-zone businesses run by NRI entrepreneurs report cancelled orders and delayed payments. Remittances from the Gulf to India, which totalled $32 billion last year, face headwinds if the slowdown persists.

Meanwhile, the roughly 650,000 Indians in Singapore are experiencing the flip side. Job postings in trade finance and logistics have risen 40 per cent in the first quarter. Indian professionals in commodity trading and supply-chain management are in high demand as firms scramble to reroute global flows.

## India's overall trade picture

The broader numbers remain mixed. India's merchandise exports hit a four-year high of $43.6 billion in April, buoyed by petroleum products and engineering goods. But the trade deficit ballooned to $28.4 billion, driven by elevated crude oil imports from Oman and Saudi Arabia — themselves a consequence of the Hormuz disruption.

Economists warn that the trade shift is not necessarily permanent. If the conflict de-escalates and insurance premiums normalise, the UAE will reclaim its position. But each month the crisis continues, the longer exporters build Singapore-centric logistics chains that may prove sticky.

## What to watch

The Indian government has so far avoided publicly acknowledging the trade rerouting, preferring to frame the April export numbers as evidence of broad-based growth. But the Commerce Ministry's internal assessments, reviewed by two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, flag Singapore's sudden prominence as a risk factor: a re-export-heavy trade profile can be reversed just as quickly as it formed.

For the diaspora, the question is more immediate. NRI business owners in Dubai and Abu Dhabi are watching the Hormuz situation with the same intensity as oil traders. Their livelihoods — and, in many cases, their residency status — depend on the free zones and trade corridors that the war is slowly strangling.
